proposal.title: Launch Aurelia-hosted AION C IDE 2.0 at NCC 1979
proposal.reason: Author-approved workflow: compile on Aurelia, save Apple-format executables on FlexiDisk II, and run natively on Apple II. Keep the 1978 1.0 edition and all existing bundles unchanged; add a separate 2.0 edition and offering. Native Apple graphics/sound/hardware libraries coexist with full contemporary Aurelia TUI/graphics semantics through Logix video. Extend event/campaign and responsible development work together. The live demonstration gains four minutes, bringing the recorded presentation total from 50 to 54 minutes. Two distribution diskettes follow the accepted C IDE default, subject to image-fit qualification.

after.name: AION C IDE 2.0 — Aurelia and Apple II targets
after.description: Aurelia-hosted C IDE retaining native Z80 development and adding native MOS 6502 output for Apple II. Save Apple-format executable disks through FlexiDisk II, then run them on Apple II. Optional Logix video provides the complete contemporary Aurelia TUI/graphics profile; separate libraries expose native Apple hardware.

composition_history.description: AION C 2.0 cross-development release at NCC 1979

chapters.description: AION C IDE integrates source editing, project/module configuration, compilation, assembly, linking, diagnostics and debugging. The editor highlights C keywords, comments, string/character literals and preprocessor lines using semantic attributes. Monochrome displays use distinguishable supported intensity/inverse attributes; selection and error emphasis remain readable. Lexical recoloring is restricted to affected visible text with bounded state for multiline comments. Disk-backed buffers support sources larger than editor working memory. Tools may execute sequentially and use overlays, preserving source, cursor and diagnostic state.

The compiler implements {language_contract_id} and libraries follow {runtime_contract_id}. Structures, typedef, function pointers, documented 32-bit integer arithmetic and shared string/stream-I/O semantics are retained. Profiles {build_profiles} build {build_targets}; later ANSI C features and future processor targets are not implied. The project records modules, include paths, libraries and debug/size/speed options, rebuilds changed modules and maps diagnostics back to source locations. Compilation executes on Aurelia or Aurelia+; Apple II is an output target, not an IDE host. Apple binaries use native MOS 6502 instructions, target startup code and libraries. The ERA/AIONix target remains a later release.

The Z80 optimizer performs constant folding and propagation, provably safe dead/unreachable-code elimination, local common-expression elimination, redundant load/store removal, branch simplification and target-specific peephole optimization. Basic-block liveness and register-pair allocation reduce memory traffic. Loop address induction and strength reduction are used when profitable; small visible function bodies may be selectively inlined under size/speed policy. Aliasing, external/assembly calls, signed arithmetic and hardware effects constrain transformations. Driver calls and declared hardware accesses are treated as observable effects. Assembly interface declarations must expose clobbers and side effects or the compiler assumes conservative barriers. No full modern whole-program optimizer is promised. Compare optimized and unoptimized outputs for identical numeric and I/O behaviour.

Performance-critical block copying/filling, string scanning/comparison, integer arithmetic, selected decimal/fixed-point operations and record comparison/search kernels are implemented in tuned Z80 assembly. Publish operation widths, precision, rounding, overflow, overlap and error rules. Link only referenced library modules; application data and writable runtime state remain in RAM. Users can assemble their own modules, create libraries and link them with C objects. Publish symbols, object/archive format, argument/return locations, preserved registers, stack rules, data layout and callback/reentrancy requirements. Supply C-to-assembly, assembly-to-C and callback examples. Interrupt handlers do not reenter non-reentrant CP/M/TUI routines. Benchmark useful operations including call and bank-switch overhead; no blanket speed or code-size guarantee.

Headers, ROM-call stubs and examples use the accepted system-cartridge TUI. Provide text fields, lists, tables, dropdown selection and buttons with consistent validation, Tab/Shift-Tab focus traversal, keyboard shortcuts, selection and copy/cut/paste. DRI owns shared clipboard storage/lifecycle; helpers obey published capacity, formats and ownership. The IDE SDK supplies composite table/dropdown helpers over existing ROM primitives when a native control is absent; this does not silently add new services to the accepted ROM image. Tables request bounded rows/pages through application callbacks. Forms use C-defined descriptors and callbacks; a visual drag-and-drop form designer is not part of this release. On Apple II, the native runtime and video-card ROM implement the same command/control semantics with host-specific clipboard storage; DRI CP/M implementation ownership is unchanged. Adapt physical keyboard shortcuts through documented aliases or menus. The S-100 ROM path requires qualified CP/M/TUI extensions.

Use {display_api} to enumerate/test/select modes and query the actual configuration. Text mode is the compact default for the IDE; generated applications can draw text/glyphs, lines, rectangles, fills and documented bitmap formats with clipping. SDK adapters render the same control model in text or bitmap mode with shared keyboard semantics; optional helper code links into the application rather than assuming every renderer is in ROM. Bitmap rendering is limited to qualified modes and memory budgets. Mode changes preserve application document/control state and trigger redraw. Do not assume simultaneous text and full bitmap buffers, readable 80 columns on every monitor, transparent conversion of old programs or hardware drawing acceleration.

Provide symbol maps, emitted source/line-to-address mappings, inspectable RAM state, RAM breakpoints and single-step for qualified builds. Optimized code may reorder or remove source operations; use debug builds for predictable stepping. XIP ROM cannot be patched with software breakpoints: use supported call stubs or qualified RAM-loaded equivalents. ROM-aware linking separates code/constants from initialized and uninitialized RAM data, provides disk/cartridge images and reports ROM/RAM usage and stack estimates. Indirect calls, recursion and assembly routines can prevent a proven stack bound and must be flagged. These inherited debugging facilities concern the Z80 host path. Apple builds include link maps and symbols for target testing; an Apple-native monitor or remote debugging service is a separately qualified tool, not implied by cross-compilation.

Supported hosts are {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}, using {runtime_cpm_aurelia}; the nominal installed-RAM minimum remains {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The 48 KiB profile publishes 40704 application bytes and the 64 KiB profile 57088 bytes under the existing reservations. These are ceilings, not spare space available to every tool. Measure editor buffers, pass overlays, library state, stack and disk intermediate files against actual reservations. A single-drive workflow may require media exchanges. Two distribution diskettes follow the recorded package definition, with image fit, working-disk requirements and installation qualification still required. No additional RAM or ROM capacity is inferred. Apple target RAM is a separate budget: publish code/data, DOS/firmware reservations, zero-page and stack use per profile. No particular Apple RAM minimum is claimed before image-fit measurement. The two-diskette packaging default remains a distribution target; added backend/library image fit must be tested.

Qualify syntax coloring and recovery from unterminated comments/strings, diagnostic navigation, incremental builds, library selection, C/assembly calls and nested bank restoration. Compare debug/optimized arithmetic and file results; test overlap, rounding, overflow and invalid inputs. Exercise forms and bitmap redraw in 40/80-column and monochrome/color configurations, clipboard-full, disk-full and exhausted-memory failures. Benchmark forms/record entry, sorting/search, decimal accounting and a bounded recalculation workload on named hardware. Report executable size, peak workspace, stack estimates, disk scratch use and build/run times. Fast libraries and advanced optimization are implementation commitments; measured superiority to earlier tools or hand-written assembly remains to be demonstrated. SSG General Ledger is an external acceptance workload: reconcile CBASIC and C financial results, measure native application work and ROM TUI overhead separately, and keep the publisher’s source and accounting rules outside the reusable IDE product.

The new backend emits native MOS 6502 code with target-specific instruction selection, local simplification and peephole optimization. Use 8-bit char, 16-bit short/int/data pointers and 32-bit long with explicit signedness/layout rules; provide software arithmetic and assembly-library kernels. Reserve zero-page locations and a software data stack separately from the processor return stack. Define C/assembly arguments, returns, clobbers, callbacks and bank restoration. Do not claim Z80 register allocation applies unchanged to 6502 or that generated code matches assembly performance. Compare optimized/debug results and measure code growth, runtime workspace and stack depth.

chapters.chapter_name: Build on Aurelia, save to Apple disk, run on Apple
chapters.description: Select the Apple target, compile/link on Aurelia and inspect target code/data/stack reports. The export tool creates or updates an Apple DOS 3.2-compatible filesystem through {transfer_drive}, writes native binary-file load-address/length headers and verifies the output. Use 13-sector media for this June 1979 release. Boot the Apple using its existing compatible DOS disk, insert the generated application disk and load/run the binary. A compatible Disk II reader needs no Logix expansion interface merely to read this disk. Directly attaching FlexiDisk II to Apple requires {apple_interface} and its disk adapter. Do not assume shared CP/M/Apple disk formats, CP/M execution on Apple or an included Apple OS boot image.

chapters.chapter_name: Portable Logix presentation and native Apple hardware
chapters.description: Programs using the common API can keep application logic, TUI descriptors and drawing calls when rebuilt for {apple_video}. The card and libraries reproduce every TUI feature and graphics mode in the June 1979 Aurelia profile on matching qualified monitors, including frames/windows, controls, text/bitmap modes and sprites. Recompile with the target ABI and replace direct Z80/Aurelia hardware access; equivalent API behaviour is not binary compatibility or a speed guarantee. Separate Apple-specific headers/libraries expose native text/graphics modes, speaker, paddles/buttons and documented peripheral hooks without requiring the Logix video card. Such calls belong in target adapters and need replacements for Aurelia. Capability checks distinguish native-video, Logix-video and optional FlexiBUS paths; errors report absent hardware instead of silently using an incompatible display.

Build the same portable console, arithmetic, file and bounded TUI workloads for Z80 and 6502 and compare semantic results and serialized data. Exercise every contemporary Aurelia control and graphics mode on Apple Logix video and qualified S-100 CP/M/TUI configurations, including focus, frames, fonts, selection, clipboard, sprites and mode-change redraw. Test native Apple graphics/speaker separately, without a Logix video dependency. Validate ROM bank restoration when alternating UI and disk calls, physical key mappings, disk-full/write-protect failures and target memory exhaustion. Demonstrate the complete Aurelia build → FlexiDisk II Apple-format disk → Apple II execution route; measured fit, throughput and regression results remain release acceptance work, not invented benchmark results.

before.title: NCC 1979 presentation and Apple II/S-100 expansion launch
before.description: On 4 June 1979, Logix holds its NCC open-architecture and migration presentation and launches the Apple II Expansion Card, FlexiDisk II, S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. An Apple representative participates in the native Apple demonstration. The cards initially use AION chips and ship with the applicable native Apple drivers/examples or supported S-100 CP/M adapters. Apple participates in the native Apple demonstration without endorsing S-100 systems.

inputs.description: The Apple technical cooperation agreement provides the documentation, test machines and compatibility assistance used for the native Apple expansion products.
The portable DRI extension release provides documented software services used in supported compatibility demonstrations and S-100 CP/M integration.

outcomes.description: The open-architecture and migration programme is presented to NCC participants; product availability and development plans remain distinguished.
The five Apple II and S-100 expansion products have a recorded launch, with initial AION chip supply and host-appropriate drivers and adapters.

after.title: NCC 1979 presentation and Apple II/S-100 expansion launch
after.description: On 4 June 1979, Logix holds its NCC open-architecture and migration presentation and launches the Apple II Expansion Card, FlexiDisk II, S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. An Apple representative participates in the native Apple demonstration. The cards initially use AION chips and ship with the applicable native Apple drivers/examples or supported S-100 CP/M adapters. Apple participates in the native Apple demonstration without endorsing S-100 systems. AION C IDE 2.0 also launches: compile on Aurelia, write native MOS 6502 executables in Apple format through FlexiDisk II, and run them on Apple II. Logix video-card ROMs and libraries reproduce the contemporary Aurelia TUI and graphics profile; separate Apple-specific libraries retain native graphics, sound and peripheral access. S-100 TUI services require qualified CP/M with TUI/Platform Extensions.

inputs.description: The Apple technical cooperation agreement provides the documentation, test machines and compatibility assistance used for the native Apple expansion products.

outcomes.description: The open-architecture and migration programme is presented to NCC participants; product availability and development plans remain distinguished.

The five expansion products and Aurelia-hosted AION C IDE 2.0 have a recorded launch. The cards supply host-specific TUI/display ROM services; the compiler adds native Apple output and a FlexiDisk II disk-transfer workflow. Product introduction does not substitute for recorded image-fit and interoperability acceptance.

before.title: NCC 1979 open architecture and migration campaign
before.objective: Encourage independent manufacturers and developers to adopt documented compatibility interfaces, and show customers how supported software, documents and peripherals can protect their investment across computer brands.
message: Choose your computer. Keep your investment.
Use documented interfaces and qualified configurations to connect products from independent suppliers.
Choose CP/M applications, FlexiBUS peripherals and display options separately; adopting one does not require the entire Logix platform.
Prepare for future computers through portable C source and documented interfaces while continuing to use and support established eight-bit systems.
audience: Business customers choosing computers, applications and peripherals.
Independent computer and peripheral manufacturers evaluating compatibility programmes.
Software publishers, developers, dealers and integrators supporting existing and future systems.

marketing_steps.description: Qualify partner claims and protect the next-generation architecture disclosure.

marketing_presentation.description: Identify shipping products, qualified configurations, prototypes and plans separately. Manufacturer interest and campaign targets are not signed agreements, verified adoption or sales.

CP/M remains commercially licensed. Non-exclusive implementation rights do not change software ownership or imply open-source licensing. Reference-code rights, certification scope and support terms must be stated before making firm offers.
Claim compatibility only for named software versions, resources, host adapters and tested configurations. Preserve each supplier’s brand, licences and support responsibilities.
Label the Model II demonstration as a prototype until customer release. AION supplies the June 1979 cards; SMC remains a future source subject to individual chip qualification.

Apple’s demonstration participation covers native Apple II products and does not endorse S-100 systems. These products provide neither Apple CP/M/Z80 execution nor automatic conversion of existing Apple graphics.

Until 19 May 1980, refer to future systems only as next-generation computers. Withhold product, processor and OS names; word size, ISA, registers, execution design, address and memory organisation; performance figures, clock rates, chip counts, schematics, board images, bus topology and future display specifications.

Keep coprocessor implementation and integration details, future-target SDKs, compiler output, binaries and revealing benchmarks confidential. Apply this embargo to presentations, questions, advertising, dealer scripts, sales proposals, OEM briefings, clinics and all attachments; current CP/M, FlexiBUS and optional display documentation may be shared.

Use released eight-bit software and explicitly identified qualified prototypes in demonstrations. Label prepared data and recordings, obtain partner clearance, and report measured resource and interoperability limits rather than implying universal performance.
Do not imply an engineering guarantee, product withdrawal date or promise that every model remains in production. Do not promise funded support for an unspecified duration.

marketing_steps.description: Demonstrate independent customer choices at NCC 1979.

marketing_presentation.description: Allow {programme_minutes} minutes for the presentation programme; questions and follow-up are separate.
Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Explain how independent software, peripheral and display choices can protect a customer’s investment.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Demonstrate an Abacus document round trip between Aurelia and the Model II prototype using separately qualified host editions. Show supported common behaviour without promising identical binaries or disk formats.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Demonstrate Abacus, then independent SSG General Ledger records and summary export. Explain the prepared data and separate licensing; do not imply that SSG has a Model II port.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Operate a qualified peripheral sequentially on named hosts. Show identification, driver support and supported application functions, attaching only when the port is quiescent.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Present the Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II alongside the S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. An Apple representative joins the native Apple demonstration. Explain the drivers, optional display hardware and separate S-100 support without suggesting Apple endorses S-100 systems.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. DRI, Tandy, Microsoft, SSG management and confirmed peripheral participants explain their responsibilities and commercial access. Distinguish current AION chip supply from prospective SMC supply and signed partners from recruitment prospects.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. {presenter} explains that future computers will not run existing Z80 binaries natively. Existing C tools and documented APIs reduce source migration work; recompilation, adaptation and testing remain necessary. Describe the planned optional Z80 coprocessor and the continuing role of eight-bit systems without revealing the new architecture.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Identify available products, prototypes and future plans. Direct customers and developers to documented configurations, licence terms, the compatibility directory and programme registration.

marketing_steps.description: Explain the separate software, peripheral and display compatibility profiles.

marketing_presentation.description: Specify the CP/M core and optional extension versions, processor instruction set, available transient-program memory, adapters and qualified applications for each configuration. Document common file formats and APIs. FlexiBUS and Logix video are optional; native displays, disks and conventional ports remain valid. Ordinary CP/M support does not guarantee every extended application, Z80 binary, file system or floppy format.

Publish electrical and transport rules, device-class profiles, host drivers, diagnostics and named qualification results. Other processors and operating systems may use their own drivers without adopting CP/M or Logix video. Device identification alone does not prove feature compatibility. Version 1 uses one device per point-to-point port, with no passive hub or daisy chain; its faster rate allows at most 50 KB/s before protocol overhead.

Separate graphics API compatibility from controller cards, the digital monitor link and qualified display modes. FlexiBUS and the full Aurelia architecture are optional. An 80-column mode needs a qualified 640-pixel monitor; adding a card does not give existing 320-pixel launch monitors that resolution.

The NCC launch covers the Apple II Expansion Card, FlexiDisk II, S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. The Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II are existing products presented alongside the three new interface/video cards. Cards initially use AION chips and include native Apple drivers and examples or supported S-100 CP/M adapters as appropriate. Keep host requirements and supplier support explicit.
Explain implementation and qualification requirements for {subject}.
Explain supported interaction behaviour under {subject}.
Present {subject} to developers implementing supported interfaces.
Explain source portability through {subject}, with recompilation and testing still required.
Distinguish graphics API compatibility under {subject} from qualified display hardware.
Explain the qualified monitor connection defined by {subject}; this is not a consumer television interface.

marketing_steps.description: Recruit independent implementers under explicit terms and governance.

marketing_presentation.description: Describe DRI’s software leadership and Logix’s hardware contribution. Invite independent computer, peripheral and software suppliers to a programme offering published specifications, versioning, backward-support policies, reference drivers, conformance tests, configuration diagnostics and a certification dispute process. Explain non-exclusive own-brand implementation, equal access to qualified components, disclosed supply priorities and manufacturer representation in a working group.

Identify the unresolved licence terms, reference-code redistribution rights, support duration and staffing, legacy-maintenance budget, working-group charter and voting rules, certification operator and scope, supply allocations, lead times and warranties. Present these as matters to settle, not existing contractual guarantees.

Invite suppliers to offer wider carriage, letter-quality printing, specialist forms and faster devices. Require the relevant status, character or graphics, paper and form-control support; the basic printer protocol does not cover every feature.
Invite business-chart and engineering-output devices, subject to a new plotting profile and suitable application support.
Invite communications and remote-access products with defined serial data, flow-control, modem-status and control profiles and host drivers.

Invite larger floppy systems, backup products and selected hard disks. Specify geometry, removable-media errors, durable writes, boot rules and measured throughput. Native faster disk controllers remain a valid choice.
Invite instruments, readers and business-input devices with published class or vendor-extension profiles and host drivers. Do not imply that foreign-processor ROM drivers execute automatically.

marketing_steps.description: Explain source migration, legacy support and the continuing eight-bit market.

marketing_presentation.description: The 4 June 1979 announcement explains source migration and the planned optional Z80 compatibility path. Full architecture disclosure is scheduled for 19 May 1980. The all-years technical catalogue is internal author material, not a 1979 press kit.

Use the established Z80 C environment, documented APIs, portable file formats and separate platform adapters. A later target needs recompilation and testing, with review of assembly code, integer and pointer assumptions, memory banking and direct hardware access. Source portability does not preserve native Z80 binary execution.

Describe an optional Z80 coprocessor planned for qualified legacy applications. Availability and compatibility are not guaranteed for every model or hardware-dependent program. Keep its implementation, interconnect, memory mapping and host integration confidential until the architecture reveal.
Maintain CP/M tools and applications alongside next-generation development. Publish a funded support duration before making a dated service promise.
Explain that eight-bit computers retain useful business roles while falling costs broaden home, education and personal use. There is no fixed date when all business customers switch platforms.

The current professional digital monitor interface cannot drive a consumer television. A computer intended to use an existing television requires separate display engineering; the basic-storage configuration remains unresolved.

marketing_steps.description: Prepare the actual transfer demonstration, venue and architecture answers.

marketing_presentation.description: Document the actual file-transfer route and floppy formats used for the Aurelia-to-Model-II round trip. Publish tested RAM and application-workspace requirements, load and recalculation times and document-capacity limits. Label prepared data and recordings and preserve independent SSG branding and participant clearances.
Use booked presentation space; main-stage access, the exact slot and audiovisual suitability require confirmation. The eight presentation stages total 50 minutes, followed by questions.

Use this response to questions seeking confidential details: We will discuss the new architecture at NCC 1980. Today we can describe our C migration approach and planned optional Z80 compatibility path.

marketing_steps.description: Evaluate manufacturer adoption against stated targets.

marketing_presentation.description: By the end of 1979, aim for Tandy shipping, one additional OEM selling a supported CP/M-extension or FlexiBUS configuration, another in qualification and verified third-party devices in several categories. By NCC 1980, aim for three to five distinct non-Logix manufacturers with supported configurations. Count Tandy once and exclude duplicate dealer builds and product variants; these are targets, not achieved results.

composition_history.description: AION C 2.0 cross-development release at NCC 1979

chapters.description: AION C IDE integrates source editing, project/module configuration, compilation, assembly, linking, diagnostics and debugging. The editor highlights C keywords, comments, string/character literals and preprocessor lines using semantic attributes. Monochrome displays use distinguishable supported intensity/inverse attributes; selection and error emphasis remain readable. Lexical recoloring is restricted to affected visible text with bounded state for multiline comments. Disk-backed buffers support sources larger than editor working memory. Tools may execute sequentially and use overlays, preserving source, cursor and diagnostic state.

The compiler implements {language_contract_id} and libraries follow {runtime_contract_id}. Structures, typedef, function pointers, documented 32-bit integer arithmetic and shared string/stream-I/O semantics are retained. Profiles {build_profiles} build {build_targets}; later ANSI C features and future processor targets are not implied. The project records modules, include paths, libraries and debug/size/speed options, rebuilds changed modules and maps diagnostics back to source locations. Compilation executes on Aurelia or Aurelia+; Apple II is an output target, not an IDE host. Apple binaries use native MOS 6502 instructions, target startup code and libraries. The ERA/AIONix target remains a later release.

The Z80 optimizer performs constant folding and propagation, provably safe dead/unreachable-code elimination, local common-expression elimination, redundant load/store removal, branch simplification and target-specific peephole optimization. Basic-block liveness and register-pair allocation reduce memory traffic. Loop address induction and strength reduction are used when profitable; small visible function bodies may be selectively inlined under size/speed policy. Aliasing, external/assembly calls, signed arithmetic and hardware effects constrain transformations. Driver calls and declared hardware accesses are treated as observable effects. Assembly interface declarations must expose clobbers and side effects or the compiler assumes conservative barriers. No full modern whole-program optimizer is promised. Compare optimized and unoptimized outputs for identical numeric and I/O behaviour.

Performance-critical block copying/filling, string scanning/comparison, integer arithmetic, selected decimal/fixed-point operations and record comparison/search kernels are implemented in tuned Z80 assembly. Publish operation widths, precision, rounding, overflow, overlap and error rules. Link only referenced library modules; application data and writable runtime state remain in RAM. Users can assemble their own modules, create libraries and link them with C objects. Publish symbols, object/archive format, argument/return locations, preserved registers, stack rules, data layout and callback/reentrancy requirements. Supply C-to-assembly, assembly-to-C and callback examples. Interrupt handlers do not reenter non-reentrant CP/M/TUI routines. Benchmark useful operations including call and bank-switch overhead; no blanket speed or code-size guarantee.

Headers, ROM-call stubs and examples use the accepted system-cartridge TUI. Provide text fields, lists, tables, dropdown selection and buttons with consistent validation, Tab/Shift-Tab focus traversal, keyboard shortcuts, selection and copy/cut/paste. DRI owns shared clipboard storage/lifecycle; helpers obey published capacity, formats and ownership. The IDE SDK supplies composite table/dropdown helpers over existing ROM primitives when a native control is absent; this does not silently add new services to the accepted ROM image. Tables request bounded rows/pages through application callbacks. Forms use C-defined descriptors and callbacks; a visual drag-and-drop form designer is not part of this release. On Apple II, the native runtime and video-card ROM implement the same command/control semantics with host-specific clipboard storage; DRI CP/M implementation ownership is unchanged. Adapt physical keyboard shortcuts through documented aliases or menus. The S-100 ROM path requires qualified CP/M/TUI extensions.

Use {display_api} to enumerate/test/select modes and query the actual configuration. Text mode is the compact default for the IDE; generated applications can draw text/glyphs, lines, rectangles, fills and documented bitmap formats with clipping. SDK adapters render the same control model in text or bitmap mode with shared keyboard semantics; optional helper code links into the application rather than assuming every renderer is in ROM. Bitmap rendering is limited to qualified modes and memory budgets. Mode changes preserve application document/control state and trigger redraw. Do not assume simultaneous text and full bitmap buffers, readable 80 columns on every monitor, transparent conversion of old programs or hardware drawing acceleration.

Provide symbol maps, emitted source/line-to-address mappings, inspectable RAM state, RAM breakpoints and single-step for qualified builds. Optimized code may reorder or remove source operations; use debug builds for predictable stepping. XIP ROM cannot be patched with software breakpoints: use supported call stubs or qualified RAM-loaded equivalents. ROM-aware linking separates code/constants from initialized and uninitialized RAM data, provides disk/cartridge images and reports ROM/RAM usage and stack estimates. Indirect calls, recursion and assembly routines can prevent a proven stack bound and must be flagged. These inherited debugging facilities concern the Z80 host path. Apple builds include link maps and symbols for target testing; an Apple-native monitor or remote debugging service is a separately qualified tool, not implied by cross-compilation.

Supported hosts are {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}, using {runtime_cpm_aurelia}; the nominal installed-RAM minimum remains {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The 48 KiB profile publishes 40704 application bytes and the 64 KiB profile 57088 bytes under the existing reservations. These are ceilings, not spare space available to every tool. Measure editor buffers, pass overlays, library state, stack and disk intermediate files against actual reservations. A single-drive workflow may require media exchanges. Two distribution diskettes follow the recorded package definition, with image fit, working-disk requirements and installation qualification still required. No additional RAM or ROM capacity is inferred. Apple target RAM is a separate budget: publish code/data, DOS/firmware reservations, zero-page and stack use per profile. No particular Apple RAM minimum is claimed before image-fit measurement. The two-diskette packaging default remains a distribution target; added backend/library image fit must be tested.

Qualify syntax coloring and recovery from unterminated comments/strings, diagnostic navigation, incremental builds, library selection, C/assembly calls and nested bank restoration. Compare debug/optimized arithmetic and file results; test overlap, rounding, overflow and invalid inputs. Exercise forms and bitmap redraw in 40/80-column and monochrome/color configurations, clipboard-full, disk-full and exhausted-memory failures. Benchmark forms/record entry, sorting/search, decimal accounting and a bounded recalculation workload on named hardware. Report executable size, peak workspace, stack estimates, disk scratch use and build/run times. Fast libraries and advanced optimization are implementation commitments; measured superiority to earlier tools or hand-written assembly remains to be demonstrated. SSG General Ledger is an external acceptance workload: reconcile CBASIC and C financial results, measure native application work and ROM TUI overhead separately, and keep the publisher’s source and accounting rules outside the reusable IDE product.

The new backend emits native MOS 6502 code with target-specific instruction selection, local simplification and peephole optimization. Use 8-bit char, 16-bit short/int/data pointers and 32-bit long with explicit signedness/layout rules; provide software arithmetic and assembly-library kernels. Reserve zero-page locations and a software data stack separately from the processor return stack. Define C/assembly arguments, returns, clobbers, callbacks and bank restoration. Do not claim Z80 register allocation applies unchanged to 6502 or that generated code matches assembly performance. Compare optimized/debug results and measure code growth, runtime workspace and stack depth.

chapters.description: Programs using the common API can keep application logic, TUI descriptors and drawing calls when rebuilt for {apple_video}. Recompile with the target ABI and replace direct Z80/Aurelia hardware access; equivalent API behaviour is not binary compatibility or a speed guarantee. Separate Apple-specific headers/libraries expose native text/graphics modes, speaker, paddles/buttons and documented peripheral hooks without requiring the Logix video card. Such calls belong in target adapters and need replacements for Aurelia. Capability checks distinguish native-video, Logix-video and optional FlexiBUS paths; errors report absent hardware instead of silently using an incompatible display.

Build the same portable console, arithmetic, file and bounded TUI workloads for Z80 and 6502 and compare semantic results and serialized data. Exercise every contemporary Aurelia control and graphics mode on Apple Logix video and qualified S-100 CP/M/TUI configurations, including focus, frames, fonts, selection, clipboard, sprites and mode-change redraw. Test native Apple graphics/speaker separately, without a Logix video dependency. Validate ROM bank restoration when alternating UI and disk calls, physical key mappings, disk-full/write-protect failures and target memory exhaustion. Demonstrate the complete Aurelia build → FlexiDisk II Apple-format disk → Apple II execution route; measured fit, throughput and regression results remain release acceptance work, not invented benchmark results.

marketing_presentation.description: Identify shipping products, qualified configurations, prototypes and plans separately. Manufacturer interest and campaign targets are not signed agreements, verified adoption or sales.

CP/M remains commercially licensed. Non-exclusive implementation rights do not change software ownership or imply open-source licensing. Reference-code rights, certification scope and support terms must be stated before making firm offers.
Claim compatibility only for named software versions, resources, host adapters and tested configurations. Preserve each supplier’s brand, licences and support responsibilities.
Label the Model II demonstration as a prototype until customer release. AION supplies the June 1979 cards; SMC remains a future source subject to individual chip qualification.

Apple’s demonstration participation covers native Apple II products and does not endorse S-100 systems. These products provide neither Apple CP/M/Z80 execution nor automatic conversion of existing Apple graphics.

Until 19 May 1980, refer to future systems only as next-generation computers. Withhold product, processor and OS names; word size, ISA, registers, execution design, address and memory organisation; performance figures, clock rates, chip counts, schematics, board images, bus topology and future display specifications.

Keep coprocessor implementation and integration details, unreleased next-generation-target SDKs, compiler output, binaries and revealing benchmarks confidential. Apply this embargo to presentations, questions, advertising, dealer scripts, sales proposals, OEM briefings, clinics and all attachments; current CP/M, FlexiBUS and optional display documentation may be shared. The released Apple II 6502 target and its June 1979 documentation may be demonstrated publicly.

Use released eight-bit software and explicitly identified qualified prototypes in demonstrations. Label prepared data and recordings, obtain partner clearance, and report measured resource and interoperability limits rather than implying universal performance.
Do not imply an engineering guarantee, product withdrawal date or promise that every model remains in production. Do not promise funded support for an unspecified duration.

marketing_steps.description: Demonstrate independent customer choices at NCC 1979.

marketing_presentation.description: Allow {programme_minutes} minutes for the presentation programme; questions and follow-up are separate.
Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Explain how independent software, peripheral and display choices can protect a customer’s investment.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Demonstrate an Abacus document round trip between Aurelia and the Model II prototype using separately qualified host editions. Show supported common behaviour without promising identical binaries or disk formats.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Demonstrate Abacus, then independent SSG General Ledger records and summary export. Explain the prepared data and separate licensing; do not imply that SSG has a Model II port.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Operate a qualified peripheral sequentially on named hosts. Show identification, driver support and supported application functions, attaching only when the port is quiescent.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Present the five Apple II/S-100 expansion products with the Apple representative. Demonstrate {compiler}: build a small shared C sample on Aurelia, write an Apple-format executable disk with {disk}, move it to Apple II and run the native 6502 result. Show the same frames, controls and graphics through {video}, then a separate example using native Apple graphics and speaker functions. Explain the optional FlexiBUS interface, required compatible monitor and qualified S-100 CP/M/TUI path. Apple participation does not endorse S-100 systems.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. DRI, Tandy, Microsoft, SSG management and confirmed peripheral participants explain their responsibilities and commercial access. Distinguish current AION chip supply from prospective SMC supply and signed partners from recruitment prospects.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. {presenter} explains that future computers will not run existing Z80 binaries natively. Existing C tools and documented APIs reduce source migration work; recompilation, adaptation and testing remain necessary. Describe the planned optional Z80 coprocessor and the continuing role of eight-bit systems without revealing the new architecture.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Identify available products, prototypes and future plans. Direct customers and developers to documented configurations, licence terms, the compatibility directory and programme registration.

marketing_steps.description: Explain the separate software, peripheral and display compatibility profiles.

marketing_presentation.description: Specify the CP/M core and optional extension versions, processor instruction set, available transient-program memory, adapters and qualified applications for each configuration. Document common file formats and APIs. FlexiBUS and Logix video are optional; native displays, disks and conventional ports remain valid. Ordinary CP/M support does not guarantee every extended application, Z80 binary, file system or floppy format.

Publish electrical and transport rules, device-class profiles, host drivers, diagnostics and named qualification results. Other processors and operating systems may use their own drivers without adopting CP/M or Logix video. Device identification alone does not prove feature compatibility. Version 1 uses one device per point-to-point port, with no passive hub or daisy chain; its faster rate allows at most 50 KB/s before protocol overhead.

Separate graphics API compatibility from controller cards, the digital monitor link and qualified display modes. FlexiBUS and the full Aurelia architecture are optional. An 80-column mode needs a qualified 640-pixel monitor; adding a card does not give existing 320-pixel launch monitors that resolution.

The NCC launch covers the Apple II Expansion Card, FlexiDisk II, S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. The Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II are existing products presented alongside the three new interface/video cards. Cards initially use AION chips and include native Apple drivers and examples or supported S-100 CP/M adapters as appropriate. Keep host requirements and supplier support explicit. AION C IDE 2.0 runs on Aurelia and cross-compiles native Apple II programs. Both video cards implement the full contemporary Aurelia TUI and graphics profile with ROM and libraries; S-100 TUI requires qualified CP/M extensions. Apple-native graphics, sound and hardware remain available through target-specific functions.
Explain implementation and qualification requirements for {subject}.
Explain supported interaction behaviour under {subject}.
Present {subject} to developers implementing supported interfaces.
Explain source portability through {subject}, with recompilation and testing still required.
Distinguish graphics API compatibility under {subject} from qualified display hardware.
Explain the qualified monitor connection defined by {subject}; this is not a consumer television interface.

marketing_steps.description: Recruit independent implementers under explicit terms and governance.

marketing_presentation.description: Describe DRI’s software leadership and Logix’s hardware contribution. Invite independent computer, peripheral and software suppliers to a programme offering published specifications, versioning, backward-support policies, reference drivers, conformance tests, configuration diagnostics and a certification dispute process. Explain non-exclusive own-brand implementation, equal access to qualified components, disclosed supply priorities and manufacturer representation in a working group.

Identify the unresolved licence terms, reference-code redistribution rights, support duration and staffing, legacy-maintenance budget, working-group charter and voting rules, certification operator and scope, supply allocations, lead times and warranties. Present these as matters to settle, not existing contractual guarantees.

Invite suppliers to offer wider carriage, letter-quality printing, specialist forms and faster devices. Require the relevant status, character or graphics, paper and form-control support; the basic printer protocol does not cover every feature.
Invite business-chart and engineering-output devices, subject to a new plotting profile and suitable application support.
Invite communications and remote-access products with defined serial data, flow-control, modem-status and control profiles and host drivers.

Invite larger floppy systems, backup products and selected hard disks. Specify geometry, removable-media errors, durable writes, boot rules and measured throughput. Native faster disk controllers remain a valid choice.
Invite instruments, readers and business-input devices with published class or vendor-extension profiles and host drivers. Do not imply that foreign-processor ROM drivers execute automatically.

marketing_steps.description: Explain source migration, legacy support and the continuing eight-bit market.

marketing_presentation.description: The 4 June 1979 announcement explains source migration and the planned optional Z80 compatibility path. Full architecture disclosure is scheduled for 19 May 1980. The all-years technical catalogue is internal author material, not a 1979 press kit.

Use the established Z80 C environment, documented APIs, portable file formats and separate platform adapters. A later target needs recompilation and testing, with review of assembly code, integer and pointer assumptions, memory banking and direct hardware access. Source portability does not preserve native Z80 binary execution. The June 1979 release also targets native Apple II 6502 code, with Apple DOS 3.2-compatible output disks written on Aurelia through FlexiDisk II. Common console/file code and Logix video API calls minimize source changes; Apple/Aurelia-specific functions remain explicit adapters.

Describe an optional Z80 coprocessor planned for qualified legacy applications. Availability and compatibility are not guaranteed for every model or hardware-dependent program. Keep its implementation, interconnect, memory mapping and host integration confidential until the architecture reveal.
Maintain CP/M tools and applications alongside next-generation development. Publish a funded support duration before making a dated service promise.
Explain that eight-bit computers retain useful business roles while falling costs broaden home, education and personal use. There is no fixed date when all business customers switch platforms.

The current professional digital monitor interface cannot drive a consumer television. A computer intended to use an existing television requires separate display engineering; the basic-storage configuration remains unresolved.

marketing_steps.description: Prepare the actual transfer demonstration, venue and architecture answers.

marketing_presentation.description: Document the actual file-transfer route and floppy formats used for the Aurelia-to-Model-II round trip. Publish tested RAM and application-workspace requirements, load and recalculation times and document-capacity limits. Label prepared data and recordings and preserve independent SSG branding and participant clearances.
Use booked presentation space; main-stage access, the exact slot and audiovisual suitability require confirmation. The eight presentation stages total 54 minutes, followed by questions.

Use this response to questions seeking confidential details: We will discuss the new architecture at NCC 1980. Today we can describe our C migration approach and planned optional Z80 compatibility path.

marketing_steps.description: Evaluate manufacturer adoption against stated targets.

marketing_presentation.description: By the end of 1979, aim for Tandy shipping, one additional OEM selling a supported CP/M-extension or FlexiBUS configuration, another in qualification and verified third-party devices in several categories. By NCC 1980, aim for three to five distinct non-Logix manufacturers with supported configurations. Count Tandy once and exclude duplicate dealer builds and product variants; these are targets, not achieved results.
